name: Cascadian Route
approach: Multi-stage approach (~11+ miles): drive to Chelan, ferry to Lucerne, bus to Holden Village, then hike to a camp at about 7,000 ft near the North Star-Bonanza col - a full day of travel and approach.
descent: Descend via the Isella Glacier, following a mostly continuous walkway of steep rock and mellow moraine at roughly two-thirds glacier height, then cross a notch in the south ridge back to base camp.
itinerary: Documented ascent used a full day (Aug 25) for the approach/travel day, followed by the climb itself; a multi-day trip overall including hike-out.

name: Oregonian Route
approach: Standard approach follows the same Lucerne ferry -> Holden Village -> hike to the North Star-Bonanza col camp used for the Soviet Route; the first-ascent party's much longer bike-and-hike approach was due to temporary ferry/road closures in 2013 and is not typical.
descent: No dedicated descent beta found; presumed similar to the Soviet Route's two-rappel descent given the routes share their upper 600 ft and summit.
itinerary: First-ascent party's push (from their high camp) took about 30 hours total including one overnight bivouac on route.

name: Northeast Face
approach: Approach via a multi-day backpack toward Park Creek Pass/the head of Park Creek (from the Thunder Creek Trail out of Colonial Creek Campground, or as part of a Buckner-area traverse), then camp near the base of the face for an alpine start.
descent: Descend via the Booker-Buckner col.

bivy.name: Thunder Basin Hiker Camp
bivy.notes: The staging camp for Booker, Storm King and Buckner from the west, and for parties continuing over the pass toward Stehekin. It sits in meadows and small trees with roughly a thousand feet of climbing still to reach the pass, and it is reliably buggy in warm weather. Because the pass is closed to camping, groups wanting to be higher have to leave the designated system entirely and take a cross-country zone permit instead. Snow lingers in the basin and on the pass well into summer, and how long is the single most variable thing about timing a trip here.
bivy.water: Creek water at the camp, dependable through the normal climbing season. Sources higher toward the pass thin out as the snow goes.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. Camping is prohibited at Park Creek Pass itself, so this is the last legal designated camp on the west approach. A portable food canister is recommended and black bears are active in the basin; canisters can be borrowed at the permit offices.
bivy.capacity: Small subalpine hiker camp near seventeen miles in; a separate stock camp sits about a mile lower and requires fording Thunder Creek. Sites are few, and this is the most contested camp in the corridor because everyone headed for the pass wants it.

bivy.name: Neve Camp
bivy.notes: Under two miles from the Colonial Creek trailhead on flat valley trail, this is the camp that exists to absorb a late arrival rather than to stage a climb. Parties driving over from the west side after work can sleep here and still be at Junction by early afternoon the next day. It is deep forest with no views, and the bugs are heavy through midsummer. Nothing about it is alpine, which is exactly its function on a corridor where the climbing is fifteen or more miles in.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek runs beside the camp and is reliable all season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required year round. Issued at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, or emailed in advance against a reservation. Roughly 60% of sites are reservable through recreation.gov (spring lottery, then a general on-sale in late April); the rest is held for walk-up and can only be claimed the day before or day of your start.
bivy.capacity: Small forested camp, reported at roughly five tent spots, spread out enough that parties are not on top of each other. Confirm the count and per-site party limit when the permit is issued.

bivy.name: Junction Camp
bivy.notes: About ten miles in, this is where the trail finally gives something back after a long forest walk, with the Boston Glacier visible through a gap in the trees. It is the natural first or second night for parties heading to Mount Logan, and the standard stopping point on the way back out from a high camp. The trail to Fisher Basin and Easy Pass leaves from here, so it also works as a hinge for loop itineraries. The climb up gains roughly a thousand feet in a bit over two miles and is the first real work of the approach.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek is the source and is dependable, but the camp sits on a bench well above it, so water means a descent and a climb back with full bottles. Arrive with enough to cook on if you get in late.
bivy.permit: Same NPS wilderness permit as the rest of the corridor. Fire rings and a privy are present here, unlike the cross-country zones higher up — but confirm current fire restrictions on the permit rather than assuming the rings mean fires are legal.
bivy.capacity: Three designated sites, one tucked away and more private than the others. A separate stock camp sits nearby. The quota is small enough that a weekend party without a reservation should have a fallback in mind.

bivy.name: Skagit Queen Camp
bivy.notes: Roughly thirteen miles up the valley, reached after a steep mile of climbing through silver fir, and the last creekside camp before the trail commits to the headwaters. Remains of early twentieth-century mining work sit just beyond the camp. The bridge over Thunder Creek in this stretch was rebuilt in recent years, but high water in the side creeks earlier in the season is still worth asking about at the permit desk.
bivy.water: Directly on Thunder Creek, reliable through the season.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required. The quota applies to the specific camp and night, so an itinerary that slips a day needs the permit amended rather than ignored.
bivy.capacity: Small hiker camp, a handful of sites. Treat capacity as tight and reserve if your schedule cannot flex by a day.

bivy.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
bivy.notes: The eastern counterpart to Thunder Basin: the last practical night before crossing Park Creek Pass from the Stehekin side, and the staging point for Buckner and Booker approached from the east. The trail above climbs through hanging meadows to the pass with good views of Goode, Buckner and Booker on the way. Coming in from Stehekin turns a very long one-way walk into a shorter approach than the roughly nineteen miles from Colonial Creek, at the cost of a lake crossing and road transport. Which side is faster depends entirely on whether the shuttle is running to the upper valley that season.
bivy.water: Park Creek is immediately adjacent and reliable.
bivy.permit: NPS wilderness permit required, covering Lake Chelan National Recreation Area as well as the park proper. Permits for an approach started from Stehekin still come through the same park system. Plan around Lake Chelan boat and shuttle schedules, since a missed connection can put you a day off your permitted itinerary.
bivy.capacity: Creekside stock camp on the Park Creek trail. Small; the neighbouring Two Mile camp downvalley was reduced to a single site by past flooding, so do not count on it as overflow.

itinerary: Multi-day: approach and establish camp near Park Creek/the base of the face; climb the face in a long single push; descend via the Booker-Buckner col to camp; hike out.

name: Northwest Route
approach: Reached via a multi-day backpack up the Thunder Creek Trail from Colonial Creek Campground to Park Creek Pass (roughly 40 miles round trip with on the order of 7,000 ft of cumulative gain including the bonus climb to Junction Camp), or as part of a Ptarmigan-style traverse linking Cascade Pass/Buckner/Park Creek Pass. From a Park Creek Pass-area camp, it is a short day-trip scramble up to the Booker-Buckner col and on to the summit.
descent: Reverse the route back over the Booker-Buckner col and down to Park Creek Pass.

name: South Ridge
approach: Drive the Cascade River Road (paved then gravel) 23.1 miles from Marblemount to the Cascade Pass Trailhead (~3,600 ft). Hike the Cascade Pass Trail 3.7 miles/1,700 ft gain to Cascade Pass (5,392 ft), then continue up the Sahale Arm Trail toward Sahale Glacier/Sahale Camp. Leave the maintained trail near Sahale Camp and descend cross-country into Horseshoe Basin as described above.
descent: Reverse the ascent route back through Horseshoe Basin to Sahale Arm and the maintained trail.

bivy.name: Sahale Camp
bivy.notes: NPS-designated high camp on the Sahale Glacier, reached via Cascade Pass and the Sahale Arm Trail; parties continue cross-country from here into Horseshoe Basin to reach Booker's south gully.
bivy.water: Snowmelt near camp early season; may require melting snow/ice late season
bivy.permit: North Cascades National Park wilderness permit — reserve via Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center
bivy.capacity: About 6 designated sites

itinerary: Most commonly done as one very long day from the Cascade Pass Trailhead (reported parties starting ~2-3am and finishing ~7:30pm when combining with Buckner), or as a 2-day trip with a permitted overnight at Pelton Basin or Sahale Glacier Camp to shorten the summit day.

name: Northeast Ridge
approach: From US-2 at the west end of Leavenworth, follow Icicle Road (Forest Road 7600) about 8 miles, then turn left onto the signed, gravel Eightmile Road. Cross Icicle Creek and climb about 1,100 ft to the large parking area at the road's end (passing the Eightmile Creek Trailhead en route). Northwest Forest Pass required.
descent: Do not reverse the Northeast Ridge. Descend the standard Prusik Pass / Druid Plateau route, then out over Aasgard Pass and down the Colchuck Lake trail. That returns you to the same parking area at the end of Eightmile Road that the approach started from, so no car shuttle is needed — it is a long loop rather than an out-and-back, on the order of 15 miles for the day.

bivy.name: Icicle Creek Road campgrounds near Eightmile Road
bivy.notes: The route is normally done in one long day from the Stuart Lake trailhead parking, so parties sleep at the car campgrounds along Icicle Creek Road near the Eightmile Road turn.
bivy.water: Seasonal; varies by campground
bivy.permit: Campground fee; reserve on Recreation.gov where offered
bivy.capacity: Developed Forest Service campgrounds with numbered sites

itinerary: Feasible as a very long single day done as a loop: ascend the NE Ridge from the Stuart Lake Trailhead parking area at the end of Eightmile Road, then descend via Prusik Pass, the Upper Enchantments, Aasgard Pass and Colchuck Lake back to the same trailhead -- about 15 miles with sustained class 3 scrambling and heavy bushwhacking. Best attempted only by strong, experienced parties; no car shuttle is needed.

waypoints.name: Cannon Mountain summit (NE Ridge route point)

name: Castle in the Sky
approach: Hannegan Trailhead up Hannegan Pass Trail, down to the Chilliwack River, then via Easy Ridge and Easy Peak, crossing the Imperfect Impasse to the Perfect Pass area, and across (or below) the Challenger Glacier to the base of the south buttress — roughly 45 minutes from a high camp to the start of climbing. A three-day itinerary with a bivy on Easy Peak is recommended given the length of the approach.
descent: Standard descent via snow and 3rd-class scrambling on the peak's south side (the same general line as the South Spur descent), not by rappelling the route.
itinerary: Day 1: Hannegan TH to an Easy Peak bivy. Day 2: Easy Ridge/Imperfect Impasse to the Perfect Pass area, approach and climb the route (long day, 12 pitches plus ~1,000 ft of scrambling). Day 3: descend and hike out (add a weather/rest day as needed).

name: La Villa
approach: Same as the Southeast Face: from Reflection Lakes (4,859 ft), take the Pinnacle Peak Trail 1.3 miles to the Pinnacle–Plummer saddle, then contour across Pinnacle's south-face scree/talus to the base of Castle's southeast side and scramble up broken ground to reach the base of the summit block. During the Plummer Peak Fire the park closed the Butter Creek Research Natural Area, south of the Pinnacle Peak Trail to the park boundary; its edge runs along the crest at The Castle, so Castle's south side and the east end of this traverse are off limits while that closure stands. Check the park's fire and closure notices before you go.
descent: Traverse right from the La Villa belay ledge to the shared, well-used top-out area on the more heavily-trafficked 5.0 line, then make the single short rappel from the fixed anchor.
itinerary: Typically a single-day, car-to-car outing; often paired with a lap up the neighboring Southeast Face and/or a visit to Pinnacle and Plummer Peaks given the shared approach.

name: Southeast Face (Standard Route)
approach: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road (or, when the road is snowed in, at the year-round Narada Falls lot). Take the signed Pinnacle Peak Trail from the south side of the road; it climbs steadily through forest and subalpine meadow for about 1.3 miles and 1,050 ft of gain to the 5,920-ft saddle between Pinnacle Peak and Plummer Peak. From the saddle, instead of continuing up Pinnacle, traverse climber's-left (east) across Pinnacle's south-facing scree/boulder field, staying around 6,000-6,200 ft, to the col between Pinnacle and Castle — roughly another half mile of cross-country travel to the base of Castle's south/southeast side. During the Plummer Peak Fire the park closed the Butter Creek Research Natural Area, south of the Pinnacle Peak Trail to the park boundary; its edge runs along the crest at The Castle, so Castle's south side and the east end of this traverse are off limits while that closure stands. Check the park's fire and closure notices before you go.
descent: Downclimb the easy 5th-class line, or make a single short (~40 ft) rappel from the slings on the rock horn at the notch, then downclimb the short class-3 section below.

bivy.name: Cougar Rock Campground
bivy.notes: For a Tatoosh trip this is the practical drive-in base, sitting between Longmire and the switchbacks up to Narada Falls and Reflection Lakes, so the morning drive to any of these trailheads is short. It runs roughly late May into early autumn and is closed the rest of the year — which puts it out of reach for exactly the season the Lane Peak gullies are in. Book it if you want a bed for a Pinnacle or Unicorn day climb without dealing with the wilderness permit system at all.
bivy.water: Potable water at the campground; no hookups at any site
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — a developed campground. Reservations through Recreation.gov during the summer peak. Park entrance fee applies separately, and the park has used timed-entry reservations for the Nisqually/Paradise corridor in recent summers, which can affect what time you can drive up.
bivy.capacity: Around 173 individual sites plus 5 group sites

bivy.name: Tatoosh cross-country zone bivy, basins below Unicorn and The Castle
bivy.notes: Continuing past Snow Lake and sleeping higher in the basin puts you under the summit blocks of Unicorn and The Castle and dodges the two-site bottleneck at the lake. It costs you the toilet and the guaranteed water, and it demands that you actually navigate to a legal spot rather than dropping the tent at the first flat bench. Snow camping is the cleanest version of this — once the pack is deep enough the surface question goes away and you are on durable ground by definition. Human waste must be packed out where there is no soil to dig in.
bivy.water: Snowmelt runnels and small tarns while the snowpack lasts; unreliable to absent by late summer, so plan to carry or to melt
bivy.permit: Wilderness permit, same system as an established camp, but issued for the cross-country zone rather than a named site. The zone rules are the constraint: camp at least a quarter mile from any trail or road and 100 ft from water, on snow or durable ground rather than meadow.
bivy.capacity: Small parties only; standard park cross-country party limits apply

bivy.name: Snow Lake Camp
bivy.notes: The only established camp close enough to matter for Unicorn Peak, sitting in the cirque directly under it, and the one Tatoosh objective where an overnight is genuinely worth the trouble. Two sites is a hard ceiling, so a weekend party without a reservation should assume it is taken. The trailhead is a short signed pullout on Stevens Canyon Road roughly a mile and a half east of Reflection Lakes, which means the camp is only reachable by car during the summer road season. Approaching Unicorn on snow in late spring is generally pleasanter than the loose slopes left behind in late summer, which argues for going early rather than for camping.
bivy.water: Snow Lake itself, immediately adjacent and reliable all season; treat it
bivy.permit: Mount Rainier NP wilderness permit, required year round. Reserve through Recreation.gov for the summer window, or take a walk-up permit in person at the Longmire Wilderness Information Center for a non-refundable fee. NO climbing cost-recovery fee applies here.
bivy.capacity: 2 designated individual tent sites, pit toilet

itinerary: A single long day from the Puget Sound area: drive to Reflection Lakes (roughly 2.5-3 hours from Seattle), scramble/climb to the summit (about 2-3 hours including the traverse and technical pitch), spend 30-60 minutes on top, and descend in 1.5-2.5 hours — a full round trip of roughly 4-6 hours car-to-car. Often combined with Pinnacle Peak and/or Plummer Peak in the same outing since the approach trail is shared.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Peak Trailhead (Reflection Lakes, Stevens Canyon Road)

name: Last Rites
approach: Same Andrews Creek/Chewuch River approach to Cathedral Pass/Upper Cathedral Lake, then toward the Cathedral-Monk gully and along the base to its left, to the open South Face.
descent: Shares the standard walk-off descent used by the South Face and Southeast Buttress routes
itinerary: Day 1: drive from the Puget Sound area (about 4.5 hours to Winthrop plus the Chewuch River Road) and hike in — strong parties do the full 17–20 miles to Upper Cathedral Lake in one long day with heavy packs, or split it with a camp partway up Andrews Creek / the Chewuch. Day 2: rest, scout the face from the lake and from the slopes toward Amphitheater Mountain, and fix the start. Day 3: climb Last Rites, descend the Southwest Route to camp. Day 4: hike out. Four days is the realistic minimum for this peak; five is comfortable and leaves a weather day.

name: Southwest Route
approach: Base at Upper Cathedral Lake (7,380 ft). Shortest way in is the Andrews Creek Trailhead (3,050 ft) at the end of the pavement on FS 51, about 22 miles north of Winthrop: Andrews Creek Trail #504 for roughly 12 miles to Andrews Pass (6,680+ ft), descend into the Spanish Creek drainage about 2 miles to the Spanish Creek Trail junction, then take the Cathedral Lakes trail (just before the cabin, on the right) about 3 miles to the lake — roughly 17 miles and about 4,800 ft of gain. Alternatives: Chewuch River Trail #510 from Thirtymile Trailhead (3,400 ft, 29 miles up FS 51/5160), about 19.9 miles and 4,900 ft of gain on gentle valley trail; and the Boundary Trail #533 from Iron Gate (6,150 ft), about 22 miles to Cathedral Pass. From camp, the climb starts 0.6 trail miles away at Cathedral Pass.
descent: Reverse the ascent route — back across the step-across, down the Class 2-3 blocks and slabs on ducks and cairns, then sandy slopes to Cathedral Pass and 0.6 miles of trail to camp. About 45 minutes.
itinerary: Day 1: drive and hike 17–20 miles to Upper Cathedral Lake. Day 2: climb the Southwest Route (a half-day round trip from camp) and, if you have the legs, Amphitheater Mountain's West Ridge across the basin. Day 3: hike out or add Remmel Mountain. Four days round trip from home is the realistic minimum; parties commonly build a 40–50 mile Cathedral Lakes loop out of it over 5 days.

waypoints.name: Andrews Creek Trailhead (Trail #504, end of pavement on FS 51)

name: Northeast Buttress
approach: Approach as for the Cathedral Pass trail/Southwest Face route via Salmon la Sac and Forest Road 4330 to the Cathedral Rock trailhead, then to Cathedral Pass, from which the Northeast Buttress is reached.
descent: Descend the south side (the ordinary Southwest Face route) back to Cathedral Pass, with a few short fourth-class sections.
itinerary: Long single day: leave the trailhead around 5-6am, at the base of the snowfield by mid-morning, seven pitches through the middle of the day, summit early-to-mid afternoon, descend the south side and hike out — expect 12-14 hours car to car. Two-day version: camp at Nosh Nosh Wahtum or near Cathedral Pass, start the climb early on day two with a light pack, and walk out that afternoon. A fast team starting around 6am can beat the afternoon heat and still have time to spare.

waypoints.name: Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) — water and campsites
Cathedral Pass / Pacific Crest Trail junction — leave the trail here for the meadow and gear cache

name: Northeast Ridge (2003 Variation)
approach: Drive to the Cathedral Rock trailhead (Trail #1345, ~3,350 ft) via I-90 Exit 80, SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald about 14.8 miles, then 12.3 miles of gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 and the NF-153 spur. Sign the free wilderness permit at the register. Hike trail #1345 past Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake, ~4,850 ft) at 2.5 miles to the Cathedral Pass / PCT junction at 5,550 ft, 4 miles in. From there the northeast side is reached the same way as the Northeast Buttress: cut across the meadow to the stand of trees (a good gear cache), then traverse under the east face across talus toward the northeast side of the peak. Note that this route begins from the top of the original Northeast Ridge route's first pitch.
descent: Descend the south side via the ordinary Southwest Face route to Cathedral Pass.
itinerary: Long day trip: trailhead by 5am, Cathedral Pass and gear cache by 8:30am, on the route by mid-morning, six pitches through the middle of the day, summit early-to-mid afternoon, south-side descent and hike out — 12-14 hours car to car. A camp at Nosh Nosh Wahtum or Cathedral Pass on the night before converts it into a comfortable two-day trip and is the more common approach for a 5.9 alpine route this far from the road.

waypoints.name: Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake) — water and campsites
Cathedral Pass / Pacific Crest Trail junction — leave the trail here for the northeast side

name: Northwest Couloir
approach: Approached the same way as the Southwest Face route, via Salmon la Sac, Forest Road 4330, and the Cathedral Rock trail to Cathedral Pass, then around toward the northwest side of the summit block. In September a cairned line crosses heather benches up the west shoulder to the couloir base; the steep loose talus alternative is slower. Going counter-clockwise round Peggy Pond reaches the rock field by a path; traversing high and clockwise through steep heather is much worse.
descent: Downclimb/rappel the couloir past the chockstone back toward Cathedral Pass.

bivy.name: Peggy's Pond — standard base camp and water source

itinerary: Best done as an overnight. Day one: hike about 5 miles to Peggy's Pond (about 2,300 ft of gain) and camp. Day two: climb the northwest couloir in a half day from camp — a party leaving camp with two hours of light remaining can be on the summit before dusk and back at the pond before dark — then pack up and walk out the same day. It also works as a long single day from the car if you are fit, and pairs naturally with Mount Daniel from the same Peggy's Pond camp.

Cathedral Pass / Pacific Crest Trail junction
Peggy's Pond — standard base camp and water source

name: Southeast Face Chimney
approach: From I-90 take Exit 80 (Roslyn/Salmon la Sac) about 1 mile west of Cle Elum. Follow Bullfrog Road to the roundabouts, then SR-903 north through Roslyn and Ronald along Cle Elum Lake, roughly 14.8 miles to the end of maintained pavement just past the Salmon la Sac guard station. Continue onto gravel Cle Elum Valley Road / FR 4330 for 12.3 miles and bear slightly left onto the short spur (NF-153) to the Cathedral Rock trailhead (Trail #1345) at about 3,350 ft. Sign the free self-issue wilderness permit at the register. The trail climbs steadily through old-growth forest, reaching Nosh Nosh Wahtum (formerly Squaw Lake, ~4,850 ft) at 2.5 miles, then opens into subalpine meadow and blueberry slopes with Cathedral Rock filling the view ahead. At about 4 miles reach Cathedral Pass (5,550 ft) and the Pacific Crest Trail junction. Leave the trail at the pass and work up the broken south/southeast slopes and talus toward the base of the tower; the chimney system is on the face directly above, left of the ground taken by the ordinary Southwest Face route. Allow roughly 2.5-3 hours trailhead to Cathedral Pass.
descent: Downclimb and rappel the ordinary Southwest Face route back to Cathedral Pass.
itinerary: Day trip (long): leave the trailhead by 5-6am, Cathedral Pass by 8:30-9am, on the summit by late morning, back at the car mid-to-late afternoon. Two-day version (more pleasant and the common choice): hike in and camp at Nosh Nosh Wahtum or at Cathedral Pass / Peggy's Pond on day one, climb early on day two and hike out the same afternoon. Camping is not permitted within 100 feet of lakes and streams; the Peggy's Pond basin is heavily used, so camp on durable ground and pack out everything.

name: East Face
approach: From the Alpental parking lot, take the Snow Lake Trail; at about 1.5 miles turn off toward Source Lake. Ascend a 3rd-class rocky gully starting around 4,200 ft, reach a small cliff around 4,800 ft, traverse through a notch, then cross a snowy basin to the base of the route around 5,500 ft. In August the turn toward the east-face basin comes just after the first switchback above Source Lake, marked by a cairn; a faint path climbs the dry waterfall gully, then trees lead to the talus field below the face.
descent: Traverse over the false summit and down the east-trending descent gully to a notch on the southeast ridge. Head partway back toward the notch until a south-facing rock gully — marked by a tree — comes into view, then make three or more rappels down the narrow, east-facing chockstone gully to the basin, using slings and rings on trees and gear.

bivy.name: Tinkham Campground, I-90 exit 42

The extra driving costs perhaps fifteen minutes on the approach next morning, which matters little against a ten-hour climbing day. bivy.name: Source Lake basin, Alpental valley
bivy.notes: The honest finding for this zone is that all three peaks are day climbs from the Alpental lot at about 3,100 ft, and almost nobody camps for them — a full car-to-car day on Chair Peak's Northeast Buttress runs 10-12 hours, The Tooth is shorter, and Guye Peak's west face is barely an approach at all. The slopes above the lake toward Chair are an active avalanche path, so this is a fair-weather summer bivy and not a winter one. bivy.permit: Free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the Snow Lake trailhead, required for day and overnight use roughly May 15 to Oct 31. Parking takes a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass, or a day fee; a Washington Discover Pass is NOT valid. Ski season changes this: on weekends and holidays the Alpental lots are run by the ski area under a paid permit, free for carpools of 3+ and for season-pass holders. No Sno-Park permit applies at Alpental.
bivy.capacity: Informal — a handful of small tent spots on durable ground; no established or designated sites

bivy.name: Chair Peak basin snow camp
bivy.notes: Parties climbing Chair Peak's north face or Northeast Buttress in winter sometimes carry up and camp in the basin near the Thumb Tack, which removes the last stretch of approach from a long summit day. Whether that is a good trade is genuinely contested: it shortens the morning but puts you sleeping under loaded avalanche slopes, and most parties instead take a 5 a.m. start from the car and accept the full approach. The elevation given is approximate for the gearing-up basin and will shift with where the snowpack lets you build a platform. Treat this as a conditions-dependent choice, not a standing campsite.
bivy.water: None running. Melt snow — this is a winter and spring option and there is no reliable liquid source in the basin.
bivy.permit: No self-issue wilderness permit is required outside roughly May 15 to Oct 31, but wilderness rules still apply and parking is governed by the ski area's winter permit scheme on peak days. Check the Alpental parking rules for the current season before counting on a spot.
bivy.capacity: Snow camp for one or two tents; no ground sites, entirely dependent on snowpack

itinerary: Single long day: alpine start from Alpental; ~2 hr approach to the Chair Peak basin; 3-pitch climb (several hours depending on party speed and conditions); rappel/downclimb descent back to the basin; hike out via Source Lake and the Snow Lake Trail.

name: Northwest Ridge
approach: Follow the East Face approach to the 'Thumbtack Rock' landmark, then head right up a grassy gully over the ridge toward the start of the Northwest Ridge.
descent: Head south over the false summits to a tree with rappel anchors at the second gully heading east, marked with slings and rings. Rappel or downclimb the gully system through to the East Face, then descend scree back to Thumbtack Rock.
